concepts.title: Covalent Bonding and Tetravalency of Carbon

questions.q: Why does carbon form covalent bonds rather than ions?
questions.a: Carbon has 4 valence electrons; gaining or losing four is too energy-costly, so it shares electrons to complete its octet.

questions.q: What is tetravalency of carbon?
questions.a: The ability of each carbon atom to form four covalent bonds with other atoms.

questions.q: Why are covalent compounds usually poor conductors and low melting?
questions.a: They have no charged particles to carry current, and weak forces between molecules need little heat to separate.

questions.q: Name the allotropes of carbon and one use of each.
questions.a: Diamond (cutting, jewellery), graphite (pencil leads, electrodes), fullerenes (research, drug carriers).

questions.q: Why can graphite conduct electricity but diamond cannot?
questions.a: Graphite has free delocalised electrons between its layers; in diamond all electrons are locked in bonds.

questions.q: What makes diamond the hardest natural substance?
questions.a: Each carbon is bonded tetrahedrally to four others forming a rigid three-dimensional network.

concepts.title: Versatile Nature of Carbon: Catenation and Tetravalency

questions.q: Why is carbon said to show catenation?
questions.a: Carbon atoms link with one another in chains, branches and rings because the C-C bond is very strong and stable.

questions.q: What is tetravalency of carbon and how does it help build many compounds?
questions.a: Each carbon forms four bonds, so it can attach to hydrogens, oxygens, nitrogen and other carbons in countless patterns.

questions.q: Do silicon and sulphur show catenation like carbon?
questions.a: Only weakly - their self-links are much weaker, which is why carbon alone builds millions of compounds.

questions.q: What are structural isomers?
questions.a: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements (structures) of atoms, like butane and isobutane.

questions.q: How many structural isomers can butane (C4H10) show?
questions.a: Two: n-butane (straight chain) and isobutane (branched chain).

questions.q: Do isomers have identical properties?
questions.a: Their molecular formula is the same but physical and some chemical properties differ because of the different structure.

What does the suffix '-ol' in an IUPAC name indicate?
questions.a: That the compound carries an alcohol (hydroxyl) functional group.

questions.q: Name the parts of an IUPAC name of an organic compound.
questions.a: A root word for the carbon chain, a primary suffix for the bond type (ane/ene/yne) and a secondary suffix or prefix for the functional group.

questions.q: What functional group does 'ethanoic acid' contain?
questions.a: The carboxylic acid group (-COOH) attached to a two-carbon chain.

concepts.title: Combustion, Oxidation, Addition, and Substitution Reactions

questions.q: What is a combustion reaction of carbon compounds?
questions.a: Burning in air giving carbon dioxide, water, heat and light - all carbon compounds burn to CO2 and H2O.

questions.q: What is an addition reaction? Give an industrial use.
questions.a: Unsaturated molecules add atoms across the double bond, e.g. hydrogenating vegetable oil with hydrogen over nickel to make ghee (vanaspati).

questions.q: What is a substitution reaction? Which hydrocarbons show it?
questions.a: One atom (usually hydrogen) is replaced by another, e.g. methane chlorinated in sunlight to chloromethane; saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) show it.

questions.q: What happens when ethanol reacts with sodium metal?
questions.a: Hydrogen gas bubbles out and sodium ethoxide forms.

questions.q: What is formed when ethanol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K?
questions.a: Ethene (an unsaturated hydrocarbon) plus water; concentrated H2SO4 acts as a dehydrating agent.

questions.q: Why is a mixture of ethanol and water called a 'tincture' when iodine is added?
questions.a: Ethanol dissolves iodine forming tincture iodine, a common antiseptic.

concepts.title: Properties and Reactions of Ethanoic Acid

questions.q: Why is ethanoic acid called a weak acid?
questions.a: It ionises only partly in water, so it gives few hydronium ions compared with strong acids like HCl.

questions.q: What is an esterification reaction?
questions.a: An acid (like ethanoic acid) reacts with an alcohol (like ethanol) in the presence of a little concentrated H2SO4 to form a sweet-smelling ester plus water.

questions.q: What is observed when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate?
questions.a: Brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide, salt (sodium ethanoate) and water form.

concepts.title: Cleansing Action of Soaps and Detergents

questions.q: How does a soap molecule clean oily dirt?
questions.a: Its hydrophobic tail sticks into oil while the hydrophilic head stays in water; micelles lift oil away so rinsing removes it.

questions.q: Why does soap not work in hard water?
questions.a: Calcium and magnesium ions of hard water react with soap forming an insoluble scum that wastes soap.

questions.q: Why do detergents work better than soaps in hard water?
questions.a: Detergent molecules do not form insoluble scum with Ca2+/Mg2+ ions, so they lather and clean even in hard water.
